chapter: Chicago in the 1920s: Bix, Armstrong, Morton
title: How cabaret pay worked: requests from singers and tips
summary: Bands got little solo time since money came from tips for numbers the singers requested; Howard recalls $56 a week plus tips.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: But did you play solo spots also, or just with the band? Bands didn't take much soles then. Not in them combinations.

And you see you only had maybe one of, maybe I'll say three or four numbers to do it if you did any at all, but them girls would get requests you know. And that's where the money's coming from. Unless somebody requests a number and pay for it and the girls didn't know it, that's when the band would play it. See? Yeah, because your money was coming from the girls singing them tables. And while-
How many of those girls were, oh you said three or three girls, right?

Well all these girls were singing, maybe one is singing, the other one's coming up and saying, as soon as you get through with me, or whatever the name is, play seven sets of things, she put the money in the box you know. And man, she's through and gone to the other girls' numbers. And she's out there singing before the girls get off the floor. All this moving. Not a dull moment. And the band played right behind those girls? Sure. And we didn't have what you call intermission. We'd get off and go to the courts, you know, and something like that. We didn't have what you call a real intermission. When did you make those- It was our interest to stay there and play, you know. Sure. It's like the Boar Rocks Club in Chicago there. The man paid us $56 a week from 1.30 to 5.30. Friday, Saturday, and Sunday morning the sun would be shining through the transom on the dance floor. You know what I'm telling you? Yes.
